title: Theorem
body_md: If $G$ is an infinite hyperbolic group, the boundary $\partial G$ admits a computably compact presentation for which the natural action of $G$ is computable.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: If $G$ is an infinite hyperbolic group, then the standard presentation of $C^*_r(G)$ is computable.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{presented metric space} is a triple $X^\#:=(X,d,(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}})$, consisting of a metric space $(X,d)$ and a countable dense sequence $(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ of $(X,d)$; in this case we also say that $X^\#$ is a \emph{presentation of $(X,d)$} and we refer to the points $x_n$ as the \emph{special points} of $X^\#$.  Such a presentation is said to be \emph{computable} if there is an algorithm such that, upon input $(m,n,k)\in \mathbb{N}^3$, returns a rational number $q>0$ such that $|d(x_m,x_n)-q|<2^{-k}$.  A computable presentation $X^\#$ of a compact metric space $(X,d)$ is \emph{computably compact} if there is an algorithm such that, upon input $k$, returns a finite sequence $i_1,\ldots,i_t\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $X$ is covered by the open balls around $x_{i_j}$ of radius $2^{-k}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{presented $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra} is a pair $(A,(a_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}})$ consisting of a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$ and a countable sequence $(a_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ from $A$ that generates $A$ as a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra; in this case, we say that $A^\#$ is a \emph{presentation of $A$} and we call the elements $a_n$ the \emph{special points} of $A^\#$.  We call the elements of $A$ of the form $p(a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_k})$, where $p$ is a $*$-polynomial with coefficients from $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, \emph{generated points} of $A^\#$; note that the generated points of $A^\#$ can be effectively enumerated and are dense in $A$.  The presentation $A^\#$ is \emph{computable} if there is an algorithm such that, upon input a generated point $a$ of $A^\#$ and rational $\epsilon>0$, returns a rational number $q>0$ such that $|\|a\|-q|<\epsilon$.
head: environment

title: Fact
body_md: Given a computably compact presentation $X^\#$ of a metric space $X$, there is a computable presentation $C(X^\#)$ of $C(X)$ that is \emph{evaluative over $X^\#$} in the sense that the evaluation map $C(X^\#)\times X^\#\to \mathbb{C}$ is computable,  meaning that there is an algorithm such that, upon input a generated point $f$ of $C(X^\#)$, $n\in \mathbb{N}$, and rational $\epsilon>0$, returns $q\in \mathbb{Q}(i)$ such that $|f(x_n)-q|<\epsilon$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{presented group} is a pair $G^\#:=(G,(g_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}})$, where $G$ is a group and $(g_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is a countable sequence in $G$ generating $G$ as a group; in this case, we say that $G^\#$ is a \emph{presentation of $G$}.  We say that the presentation $G^\#$ is \emph{computable} if there is an algorithm such that, upon input a finite word in the sequence $(g_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$, determines whether or not the word equals the identity in $G$.
head: environment

label: exacttheorem
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{exacttheorem}
Suppose that $G\curvearrowright^\alpha X$ is an amenable action of the group $G$ on the compact space $X$.  Furthermore, assume that $G^\#$ is a computable presentation of $G$, $X^\#$ is a computably compact presentation of $X$, and $G^\#\curvearrowright^\alpha X^\#$ is a computable action.  Then the presentation $C^*_r(G^\#)$ is computable.
head: environment

label: maintheorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{maintheorem}
Suppose that $G$ is an infinite hyperbolic group and that $G^\#$ is the presentation of $G$ associated to some finite generating set of $G$.  Then there is a computable presentation $\partial G^\#$ of the boundary $\partial G$ of $G$ such that the natural action of $G^\# \curvearrowright \partial G^\#$ is computable.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: If $G$ is an infinite hyperbolic group with presentation $G^\#$ associated to some finite generating set of $G$, then the corresponding presentation $C^*_r(G^\#)$ is computable.
head: environment

title: Question
body_md: Which exact groups admit computable presentations and computable, amenable actions on computably compact spaces?

label: def:cts
title: Definition
head: environment

label: msexample
title: Example
body_md:
\label{msexample}
Suppose $X^\#=(X,d,(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}})$ is a computable metric space.  From it one can obtain a computable topological space $(X,(B_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ whose numbered basis is an effective enumeration of the open balls with centers coming from the sequence $(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ and rational radii.  In what follows, we will always treat computable metric spaces as computable topological spaces in this way.  Note that the notions defined above (effectively open, effectively closed, computable point, computable map) agree with the corresponding notions from computable metric space theory, whence no confusion can arise.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
\leavevmode
Let $(X,(B_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ be a computable topological space.  We say that $X$ is
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{computably compact} if it is compact and
\[
\operatorname{Cov}:=\{\langle i_1,\dots,i_n\rangle : X=B_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup B_{i_n}\}
\]
is c.e. 
\item \emph{computably Hausdorff} if the complement of the diagonal is effectively open in $X\times X$, that is, there is a c.e.\ set $W$ of pairs $(i,j)$ such that $$\{(x,y)\in X\times X:x\ne y\}=\bigcup_{(i,j)\in W}B_i\times B_j.$$
\item \emph{computably overt} if $\{i:B_i\ne\emptyset\}$ is c.e.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: lem:proj
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:proj}
Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are computable topological spaces with $X$ computably compact.  Further suppose that $Z\subseteq X\times Y$ is effectively closed.  Then $\operatorname{proj}_Y(Z)$ is effectively closed, uniformly in all of the relevant data.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Note that $y\notin\operatorname{proj}_Y(Z)$ if and only if $X\times\{y\}\subseteq(X\times Y)\setminus Z$. By compactness of $X$ this holds if and only if finitely many basic boxes cover $X\times\{y\}$ inside the complement, and the search for such a finite family is an enumeration.
head: environment

label: lem:image
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For (1), by surjectivity, $Y=\bigcup_t B^Y_{j_t}$ if and only if $X=\bigcup_t f^{-1}(B^Y_{j_t})$, and each $f^{-1}(B^Y_{j_t})$ is effectively open uniformly because $f$ is computable; now apply computable compactness of $X$. Similarly, for (2), $B^Y_j\ne\emptyset$ if and only if $f^{-1}(B^Y_j)\ne\emptyset$, which is semi-decidable by the computable overtness of $X$.
head: environment

label: lem:graph
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:graph}
Let $f:X\to Y$ be computable with $Y$ computably Hausdorff. Then the graph of $f$ is effectively closed in $X\times Y$. If moreover $X$ is computably compact, then $f$ maps effectively closed sets to effectively closed sets, and uniformly so.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
With $W$ the Hausdorff witness set for $Y$, we have
\[
\{(x,y)\in X\times Y : y\ne f(x)\}=\bigcup_{(j,k)\in W} f^{-1}(B^Y_j)\times B^Y_k,
\]
which is effectively open. For the second claim, $f(C)=\operatorname{proj}_Y\big(\mathrm{graph}(f)\cap(C\times Y)\big)$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:proj} applies.
head: environment

label: cor:inverse
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:inverse}
A computable bijection from a computably compact space to a computably Hausdorff space has computable inverse.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For basic open $B_i\subseteq X$, bijectivity gives $f(B_i)=Y\setminus f(X\setminus B_i)$, and $f(X\setminus B_i)$ is effectively closed by Lemma~\ref{lem:graph}. So $(f^{-1})^{-1}(B_i)=f(B_i)$ is effectively open uniformly in $i$.
head: environment

label: lem:quotient
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider $\pi(x)\in V$ with $V\subseteq Y$ open. Then $\pi^{-1}(V)$ is a saturated open set containing the compact set $R[x]$, whence finitely many basic sets contained in $\pi^{-1}(V)$ cover $R[x]$; let $A$ index them. Then $R[x]\subseteq B_A\subseteq\pi^{-1}(V)$, so $\pi(x)\in C_A\subseteq V$.

Next note that $\pi^{-1}(C_A)=X\setminus R[X\setminus B_A]$. For effectively closed $C$, we have
\[
R[C]=\operatorname{proj}_2\big({\sim}\cap(C\times X)\big),
\]
which is effectively closed uniformly by Lemma~\ref{lem:proj}.  Hence $\pi^{-1}(C_A)$ is effectively open uniformly in $A$, which is computability of $\pi$.  Note in particular that this shows that each $C_A$ is open.

Declare $(C_A,C_B,C_C)\in\operatorname{Incl}_Y$ when $\operatorname{Incl}_X$ certifies $B_C\subseteq B_A\cap B_B$, that is, when, for each $k\in C$, there are $i\in A$ and $j\in B$ such that $(i,j,k)\in \operatorname{Incl}_X$.  Note that $\operatorname{Incl}_Y$ is indeed c.e. Soundness holds because $\ast$ is monotone and meet-preserving. Richness holds because the basis argument above, applied to $V=C_A\cap C_B$, produces exactly such a $C$.  

At this point, we have established (1) and (2).  (3) and (4) follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:image}.
head: environment

label: thm:metrize
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:metrize}
A computably compact, computably Hausdorff, computably overt computable topological space admits a computable metric space presentation computably equivalent to the given one.
head: environment

label: cor:quotmetrize
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:quotmetrize}
Let $X$ be a computably compact and computably overt computable topological space.  Let $\sim$ be an effectively closed equivalence relation. Equip the quotient space $Y = X/\sim$ with the above effective quotient presentation constructed from finite unions of basic opens. If $Y$ is computably Hausdorff, then $Y$ has a computably equivalent computably compact metric space presentation, and the quotient map $q:X\to Y$ is computable.
head: environment

label: Piscompcomp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Piscompcomp}
The standard presentation of $P$ is computably compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: That the presentation is computable is immediate from the definition.  To verify computable compactness, fix $n$ and for each $x\in P_n$, search for geodesic words extending $x$ that eventually reach the same state twice and use the same argument as above to compute an eventually periodic word $\alpha_x$ extending $x$.  Then for any infinite word $\alpha$, setting $x(\alpha):=\alpha(1)\cdots\alpha(n)\in P_n$, we have $d(\alpha,\alpha_{x(\alpha)})\leq 2^{-n}$.  It follows that the open balls with centers $\alpha_x$, for $x\in P_n$, and radius $2^{-n}$, form a finite open cover of $P$.
head: environment

label: lem:ft
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{lem:ft}
For $\alpha,\beta\in P$, we have that $\alpha\sim \beta$ if and only if $d(\alpha(t),\beta(t))\le 2\delta$ for all $t\ge 0$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: $\sim$ is an effectively closed equivalence relation on $P$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given Fact \ref{lem:ft}, the lemma follows from the equality
$$\{(\alpha,\beta)\in P\times P \ : \ \alpha\not\sim\beta\}=\bigcup_{t\in \mathbb{N}}\{(\alpha,\beta)\in P\times P \ : \ d(\alpha(t),\beta(t))>2\delta\}.\qedhere$$
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: Equip $\partial G$ with the computable topology it obtains from $P$ and $\sim$ as in Lemma \ref{lem:quotient}.  Then $\partial G$ is computably compact and computably overt and the quotient map $\pi:P\to \partial G$ is computable.
head: environment

label: lem:basis
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (1) follows from the fact that $$(U_F)^\ast=\{\xi\in \partial G : \pi^{-1}(\xi)\subseteq U_F\}=\{\xi\in \partial G : T_n(\xi)\subseteq F\}=B_{n,F}.$$  (2) follows from (1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient}.  It is clear that the $U_F$ are cofinal among finite unions of basic sets of $P$, and thus the $B_{n,F}$ are cofinal among the sets $C_A$; (3) now follows again from Lemma~\ref{lem:quotient}.  For (4): $T_n(\xi)\subseteq B(\alpha(n),2\delta)$ by Fact~\ref{lem:ft}, whence $\xi\in B_{n,F}$.
head: environment

label: prop:hausdorff
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:hausdorff}
Let $W$ be the decidable set of pairs of pairs $((n,F),(n,F'))$, with $F,F'\subseteq P_n$ and $F\cap F'=\emptyset$.  Then 
$$\{(\xi,\eta)\in \partial G\times \partial G \ : \ \xi\not=\eta\}=\bigcup_{((n,F),(n,F'))\in W} B_{n,F}\times B_{n,F'}.$$
Consequently, $\partial G$ is computably Hausdorff.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The inclusion ``$\supseteq$'' is obvious.  We now prove the inclusion ``$\subseteq$.''  Towards that end, consider $\xi\ne\eta$ and fix $\alpha,\beta\in P$ with $\pi(\alpha)=\xi$ and $\pi(\beta)=\eta$. Since $\alpha\not\sim \beta$, we may pick $n$ with $d(\alpha(n),\beta(n))>4\delta$ and set $F:=B(\alpha(n),2\delta)\cap P_n$, $F':=B(\beta(n),2\delta)\cap P_n$. Then $\xi\in B_{n,F}$ and $\eta\in B_{n,F'}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:basis}, and $F\cap F'=\emptyset$ by the triangle inequality.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: There is a computably compact presentation $\partial G^\#$ of $\partial G$ as a metric space so that the canonical quotient map $\pi:P\to \partial G$ is a computable map.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: It can be shown that the special points of the computable presentation of $\partial G^\#$ can be taken to be the images under $\pi$ of the eventually periodic elements of $P$.  Indeed, these points are uniformly computable and dense since these same assertions hold of the eventually periodic points in $P$.
head: environment

label: basepointfact
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{basepointfact}
Suppose that $\gamma$ is a geodesic ray in $\Gamma$ starting at $g$.  Then there is $\alpha\in P$ in $\Gamma$ starting at $e$ such that the Hausdorff distance of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ is at most $|g|+2\delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For each $n$, choose a geodesic word $w_n$ from $e$ to $\gamma(n)$.  By a K\"onig's lemma argument, we may choose a sequence $(u_k)_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ such that each $u_k$ is a prefix of $w_n$ for infinitely many $n$, each $u_k$ is a prefix of $u_{k+1}$, and the lengths of $u_k$ tend to $\infty$.  Let $\alpha\in P$ denote the geodesic ray given by the limit of this sequence.  It is a calculation using thinness to show the claimed upper bound on the Hausdorff distance between $\alpha$ and $\gamma$.
head: environment
name: Proof sketch

label: lem:basepoint
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:basepoint}
Let $\xi\in\partial G$ and suppose $\alpha\in P$ is such that $\pi(\alpha)=\xi$. Suppose also that $\gamma$ is a geodesic ray starting at $g\in G$ and staying within a finite Hausdorff distance of $\alpha$. Then for every $t>|g|+\delta$, there is $s$ with $|s-t|\le|g|+\delta$ and $d(\gamma(t),\alpha(s))\le 3\delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Fix $n\geq t$ and consider the triangle $e,g,\gamma(n)$ with sides a geodesic $[e,g]$, $\gamma|_{[0,n]}$, and a geodesic $w_n$ connecting $e$ and $\gamma(n)$. For $t>|g|+\delta$, we have $d(\gamma(t),[e,g])\ge t-|g|>\delta$, so $\gamma(t)$ is within $\delta$ of $w_n$.  Letting $\alpha'\in P$ be constructed from the sequence $(w_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ as in the proof of Fact \ref{basepointfact}, we have that $d(\gamma(t),\alpha'(s))\le\delta$ for some $s$ which necessarily satisfies $|s-t|\leq |g|+\delta$.  By Fact~\ref{lem:ft}, $d(\alpha'(s),\alpha(s))\le2\delta$, finishing the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:shrink
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:shrink}
Fix $D\ge0$ and $\zeta\in\partial G$. Let $N\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ be infinite and suppose that, for each $n\in N$, we are given $F_n\subseteq P_n$ with
\[
T_n(\zeta)\subseteq F_n \qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{diam} F_n\le D .
\]
Then $\{B_{n,F_n}\}_{n\in N}$ is a neighborhood basis at $\zeta$ consisting of open sets.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each $B_{n,F_n}$ is open and contains $\zeta$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:basis}.  Suppose, towards a contradiction, that the family is not a neighborhood basis, that is, some open $U\ni\zeta$ contains no $B_{n,F_n}$.  As a result, for each $n\in N$, there is $\eta_n\in B_{n,F_n}\setminus U$. For each $n\in N$, choose $\beta_n\in P$ such that $\pi(\beta_n)=\eta_n$.  Choose also $\alpha\in P$ such that $\pi(\alpha)=\zeta$.  Note that $d(\alpha(n),\beta_n(n))\le D$.

Fix $t$ and take $n\in N$ with $n>t+D+\delta$. Consider the geodesic triangle with vertices $e$, $\alpha(n)$, $\beta_n(n)$, two of whose sides are $\alpha|_{[0,n]}$ and $\beta_n|_{[0,n]}$. Every point of the third side has distance at least $n-D$ from $e$, so $d\big(\beta_n(t),[\alpha(n),\beta_n(n)]\big)\ge n-D-t>\delta$. Thinness therefore places $\beta_n(t)$ within $\delta$ of $\alpha([0,n])$, say $d(\beta_n(t),\alpha(s))\le\delta$; then $|t-s|=\big||\beta_n(t)|-|\alpha(s)|\big|\le\delta$ and so $d(\beta_n(t),\alpha(t))\le2\delta$.

By compactness of $P$, we may pass to a subsequence $(\beta_{n_k})_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ with $\beta_{n_k}\to\beta\in P$ in the prefix metric. For each fixed $t$, we have $\beta_{n_k}(t)=\beta(t)$ for large $k$, and the previous paragraph applies once $n_k>t+D+\delta$, so $d(\beta(t),\alpha(t))\le2\delta$ for every $t$. Hence $\beta\sim\alpha$.  Since $\pi$ is continuous, we have $\eta_{n_k}=\pi(\beta_{n_k})\to\pi(\beta)=\zeta$.  Since $\partial G\setminus U$ is closed, we have $\zeta\notin U$, which is a contradiction.
head: environment

label: inclusiondecidable
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{inclusiondecidable}
The set of pairs of pairs $$\{((n,F),(n',F')) \ : \  B_{(n,F)}\subseteq B_{(n',F')}\}$$ is decidable.
head: environment

label: prop:action
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:action}
The action of $G^\#$ on $\partial G^\#$ is computable.
head: environment

label: eq:transport
title: Proof
body_md:
We need to describe an algorithm which, given a word representing $g$ and a name of $\xi\in\partial G$, enumerates a name of $g\xi$.  Take $\alpha,\alpha'\in P$ such that $\pi(\alpha)=\xi$ and $\pi(\alpha')=g\xi$, noting that $\alpha'$ is within finite Hausdorff distance of the geodesic $t\mapsto g\alpha(t)$ beginning at $g$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:basepoint} applied with $\gamma=g\alpha$ gives, for $n>|g|+\delta$, an $s$ with $|s-n|\le|g|+\delta$ and $d(g\alpha(n),\alpha'(s))\le3\delta$, from which it follows that $d(g\alpha(n),\alpha'(n))\le4\delta+|g|$. As $\alpha'$ was arbitrary, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:transport}
T_n(g\xi)\ \subseteq\ B\big(g\alpha(n),\,4\delta+|g|\big)\cap P_n\qquad(n>|g|+\delta).
\end{equation}

Now, given a name of $\xi$, enumerate the indices $(n,F)$ with $\xi\in B_{n,F}$, and retain those with $n>|g|+\delta$ and $\operatorname{diam} F\le4\delta$, a decidable procedure. By the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:basis}, the index $\big(n,B(\alpha(n),2\delta)\cap P_n\big)$ is retained for \emph{every} such $n$, so the retained indices occur at an infinite set $N$ of levels. For each retained $(n,F)$, pick any $x\in F$; since $\alpha(n)\in T_n(\xi)\subseteq F$ and $\operatorname{diam} F\le4\delta$, we have $d(x,\alpha(n))\le4\delta$, hence $d(gx,g\alpha(n))\le4\delta$, and \eqref{eq:transport} gives
\[
T_n(g\xi)\ \subseteq\ F'_n:=B\big(gx,\,8\delta+|g|\big)\cap P_n .
\]
Output the index $(n,F'_n)$; thus $g\xi\in B_{n,F'_n}$.

We have $\operatorname{diam} F'_n\le D:=2(8\delta+|g|)$, a bound independent of $n$, and $T_n(g\xi)\subseteq F'_n$ for all $n\in N$. Lemma~\ref{lem:shrink} therefore makes $\{B_{n,F'_n}\}_{n\in N}$ a neighborhood basis at $g\xi$ of open sets.  

A name of $g\xi$ must enumerate every $j$ with $g\xi\in B_j$. Run the outputs $B_{n,F'_n}$ against all indices $j$, enumerating $j$ as soon as $B_{n,F'_n}\subseteq B_j$ is certified; since the inclusion relation is decidable by Theorem \ref{inclusiondecidable} (c.e. would suffice here), this is indeed possible.  This produces the desired name of $g\xi$.
head: environment

label: lem:key
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:key}
   Let $\alpha\in P$. Then $\alpha\in E_{n,F}$ if and only if the partner component of the run of $\mathcal D_{n,F}$ on $\alpha$ is nonempty at every step.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be the set of finite words $v$ over $S$, say of length $t$, such that (i) $v$ is geodesic, (ii) $d(\alpha(s),v(s))\le2\delta$ for all $s\le t$, and (iii) if $t\ge n$, then $v(n)\notin F$. Note that $T$ is a finitely branching tree under prefixes.

An induction on $t$ shows that the partner component of the run at time $t$ is exactly the set of endpoints $\{\bar v : v\in T,\ |v|=t\}$ in phase 1 (where $\bar v$ denotes the element of $G$ represented by $v$), and its image under $v\mapsto(\operatorname{ct}(\bar v),\alpha(t)^{-1}\bar v)$ in phase 2. In particular, the partner component is nonempty at time $t$ if and only if $T$ has a node at level $t$.

If $\alpha\in E_{n,F}$, a witness $\beta$ has all its prefixes in $T$, so $T$ has nodes at every level. Conversely if $T$ has nodes at every level then, being an infinite finitely branching tree, it has an infinite branch $\beta$ by K\"onig's lemma. All prefixes of $\beta$ are geodesic, so $\beta\in P$; condition (ii) gives $\beta\sim\alpha$; condition (iii) gives $\beta(n)\notin F$. Hence $\alpha\in E_{n,F}$.
head: environment

label: lem:refine
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:refine}
Given $k_1,\dots,k_p\in \mathbb{N}$ and a point $x\in B_{k_1}\cap\cdots\cap B_{k_p}$, one can find $i\in \mathbb{N}$ with $x\in B_i$ and $i\le^\ast k_t$ for every $t$. The search terminates whenever such an $x$ exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Richness of $\operatorname{Incl}$ applied to $x\in B_{k_1}\cap B_{k_1}$ gives $m_1$ with $x\in B_{m_1}$ and $m_1\le k_1$. Inductively, richness applied to $x\in B_{m_{t-1}}\cap B_{k_t}$ gives $m_t$ with $x\in B_{m_t}$, $m_t\le m_{t-1}$ and $m_t\le k_t$. Then $i:=m_p$ satisfies $i\le^\ast k_t$ for every $t$ by transitivity.
head: environment

label: lem:prec-down
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:prec-down}
If $A\prec B$ with witness $E$, and $A'$ is a formal open such that every $i'\in A'$ satisfies $i'\le^\ast i$ for some $i\in A$, then $E$ also witnesses $A'\prec B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: $\mathrm{Ap}(A,E)$ gives $\mathrm{Ap}(i,j)$ for $i\in A$, $j\in E$, and $\mathrm{Ap}(\cdot,\cdot)$ is downward closed in its first argument, so $\mathrm{Ap}(i',j)$.
head: environment

label: lem:prec-sound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:prec-sound}
If $E$ witnesses $A\prec B$ then $\overline{B_A}\subseteq X\setminus B_E\subseteq B_B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By definition, we have $B_A\cap B_E=\emptyset$, so $B_A\subseteq X\setminus B_E$, which is closed, whence $\overline{B_A}\subseteq X\setminus B_E$. Since $X=B_B\cup B_E$, we have $X\setminus B_E\subseteq B_B$.
head: environment

label: lem:rich
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:rich}
Let $B$ be a formal open and $x\in B_B$. Then there is $i$ with $x\in B_i$ and $\{i\}\prec B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $y\in X\setminus B_B$, there is $(k_y,l_y)\in W$ with $x\in B_{k_y}$, $y\in B_{l_y}$. The sets $B_{l_y}$ cover the compact set $X\setminus B_B$, so finitely many suffice: say $E:=\{l_1,\dots,l_p\}$ with $X=B_B\cup B_E$, and with associated $k_1,\dots,k_p$ all containing $x$. (If $X=B_B$ take $E=\emptyset$ and any $i$ with $x\in B_i$.)

By Lemma~\ref{lem:refine}, there is $i$ with $x\in B_i$ and $i\le^\ast k_t$ for all $t$. Since $(k_t,l_t)\in W$ and $l_t\le^\ast l_t$, we get $\mathrm{Ap}(i,l_t)$ for every $t$, that is $\mathrm{Ap}(\{i\},E)$. It follows that $E$ witnesses $\{i\}\prec B$.
head: environment

label: lem:union
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:union}
From witnesses for $A_1\prec B,\dots,A_r\prec B$, one can compute a witness for $A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_r\prec B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E_s$ witness $A_s\prec B$. Then $X\setminus B_B\subseteq B_{E_s}$ for each $s$, so $$X\setminus B_B\subseteq\bigcap_s B_{E_s}=\bigcup_{\vec e\,\in\,E_1\times\cdots\times E_r}\ \bigcap_{s}B_{e_s}.$$

By Lemma~\ref{lem:refine}, each $\bigcap_s B_{e_s}$ is the union of those basic $B_m$ with $m\le^\ast e_s$ for all $s$. Hence the c.e.\ family
\[
\mathcal G:=\big\{\,m\in \mathbb{N}\ :\ \text {there is }\vec e\in E_1\times\cdots\times E_r \text{ with } m\le^\ast e_s \text{ for all } s\,\big\}
\]
has $\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal G}B_m=\bigcap_s B_{E_s}\supseteq X\setminus B_B$. Since $X\setminus B_B$ is effectively closed and $\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal G}B_m$ effectively open, computable compactness produces a finite $E\subseteq\mathcal G$ with $X=B_B\cup B_E$.

It remains to check $\mathrm{Ap}(A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_r,E)$. Let $i\in A_s$ and $m\in E$, and let $\vec e$ witness $m\in\mathcal G$. Then $\mathrm{Ap}(i,e_s)$ because $\mathrm{Ap}(A_s,E_s)$ and $e_s\in E_s$; since $m\le^\ast e_s$, downward closure of $\mathrm{Ap}(\cdot,\cdot)$ in its second argument gives $\mathrm{Ap}(i,m)$.
head: environment

label: lem:interp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:interp}
From a witness for $A\prec B$, one can compute a formal open $C$ and witnesses for
\[
A\prec C\prec B .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E$ witness $A\prec B$ and put $Z:=X\setminus B_E$, an effectively closed set, with $Z\subseteq B_B$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:prec-sound}.

The family $\{B_i:\{i\}\prec B\}$ is effectively enumerable, its index set being c.e.\ because $\prec$ is c.e.. It covers $Z$ as any $z\in Z$ lies in $B_B$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:rich} supplies a suitable $i$ with $\{i\}\prec B$ and $z\in B_i$. By computable compactness, one can compute a finite $C$ with $Z\subseteq B_C$ and $\{i\}\prec B$ for each $i\in C$.

It follows that $C\prec B$, with a witness computed by Lemma~\ref{lem:union}. Note also that $E$ itself witnesses $A\prec C$: we already have $\mathrm{Ap}(A,E)$, and $X=B_C\cup B_E$ because $X\setminus B_E=Z\subseteq B_C$.
head: environment

label: lem:urysohn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:urysohn}
From a witness for $A\prec B$, one can find $f:X\to[0,1]$ with $f\equiv0$ on $B_A$ and $f\equiv1$ off $B_B$, such that $\{f<q\}$ and $\{f>q\}$ are effectively open uniformly in the witness for $A\prec B$ and $q\in\mathbb{Q}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $A_0:=A$ and $A_1:=B$ and, using Lemma~\ref{lem:interp} repeatedly, compute formal opens $A_q$ for all dyadic rationals $q\in[0,1]$ with $A_q\prec A_{q'}$, and witnesses $E(q,q')$, whenever $q<q'$. Define
\[
f(x):=\inf\{q : x\in B_{A_q}\}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:prec-sound}, the $B_{A_q}$ increase with $q$, so $f$ is well defined, vanishes on $B_{A_0}=B_A$, and equals $1$ off $B_{A_1}=B_B$.

Since $\{f<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q}B_{A_{q'}}$ and
\[
\{f>q\}=\bigcup_{q<q'<q''}B_{E(q',q'')} ,
\]
both are clearly effectively open. To see the latter equality, note that if $x\in B_{E(q',q'')}$, then $x\notin B_{A_{q'}}$ by $\mathrm{Ap}(A_{q'},E(q',q''))$, so $f(x)\ge q'>q$.  Conversely, if $f(x)>q$, choose $q<q'<q''<f(x)$, so $x\notin B_{A_{q''}}$ and hence $x\in B_{E(q',q'')}$ because $X=B_{A_{q''}}\cup B_{E(q',q'')}$.
head: environment

label: prop:metricfn
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:metricfn}
$\rho$ is a computable metric on $X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since the series converges effectively, $\rho$ is computable.  It is clearly a pseudometric.  To see that it separates points, suppose $x\ne y$ and take $(j,l)\in W$ with $x\in B_j$, $y\in B_l$; Lemma~\ref{lem:rich} applied to $x\in B_{\{j\}}$ gives $i$ with $x\in B_i$ and $\{i\}\prec\{j\}$, and the corresponding $f$ has $f(x)=0$, $f(y)=1$ since $y\notin B_j$. Hence $\rho(x,y)>0$.
head: environment

label: lem:small
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first note that such $W_{n,a,b}$ exist: take any c.e.\ index set for the effectively open $f_n^{-1}(a,b)$ (available by Lemma~\ref{lem:urysohn}) and close it under $\le^\ast$, which changes neither the union nor c.e.-ness. Closure and c.e.-ness of $\mathrm{Small}(k)$ follow.

For the diameter bound, fix $i\in\mathrm{Small}(k)$. Since $f_n$ is continuous, we have $$\overline{B_i}\subseteq\overline{f_n^{-1}(a_n,b_n)}\subseteq f_n^{-1}[a_n,b_n],$$ so $f_n$ varies by at most $2^{-k}$ on $\overline{B_i}$ for each $n\le k$. Hence, for $x,y\in\overline{B_i}$, we have
\[
\rho(x,y)\le\ 2^{-k}\sum_{n\le k}2^{-n}+\sum_{n>k}2^{-n}\ \le\ 2^{-k+1}+2^{-k}\ \le\ 2^{-k+2}.
\]

For the last point, fix $x\in X$ and $k\in \mathbb{N}$. For each $n\le k$ continuity gives rationals $a_n<f_n(x)<b_n$ with $b_n-a_n<2^{-k}$, and then some $j_n\in W_{n,a_n,b_n}$ with $x\in B_{j_n}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:refine} produces $i$ with $x\in B_i$ and $i\le^\ast j_n$ for every $n\le k$; by closure under refinement, $i\in W_{n,a_n,b_n}$ for each $n\le k$, establishing that $i\in\mathrm{Small}(k)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Omega=\{i\in\mathbb{N}:B_i\ne\emptyset\}$ be the c.e.\ set given by overtness and let $\rho$ be as in Proposition~\ref{prop:metricfn}.

Let $i_0\in\Omega$ be given. Build indices $i_1,i_2,\dots$ such that, for every $m\ge1$, we have
\[
\{i_m\}\prec\{i_{m-1}\},\qquad i_m\in\mathrm{Small}(m),\qquad i_m\in\Omega ,
\]
together with witnesses. At stage $m$, pick $x\in B_{i_{m-1}}$ (nonempty, as $i_{m-1}\in\Omega$). Lemma~\ref{lem:rich} gives $i'$ with $x\in B_{i'}$ and $\{i'\}\prec\{i_{m-1}\}$; Lemma~\ref{lem:small} gives $j\in\mathrm{Small}(m)$ with $x\in B_j$; Lemma~\ref{lem:refine} gives $i_m$ with $x\in B_{i_m}$, $i_m\le^\ast i'$ and $i_m\le^\ast j$. Then $i_m\in\mathrm{Small}(m)$ by closure under refinement, $\{i_m\}\prec\{i_{m-1}\}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:prec-down}, and $i_m\in\Omega$ since $x\in B_{i_m}$, this last being confirmed by the overtness enumeration after finitely many steps. So all three conditions are simultaneously achievable, and the search for a triple satisfying them terminates.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:prec-sound}, $\overline{B_{i_m}}\subseteq B_{i_{m-1}}$, so the sets $\overline{B_{i_m}}$ are nested; each is nonempty since $i_m\in\Omega$; and by compactness of $X$ we have $\bigcap_m\overline{B_{i_m}}\ne\emptyset$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:small}, $\operatorname{diam}_\rho(\overline{B_{i_m}})\le2^{-m+2}$, whence the intersection is a singleton, which we denote by $x^\ast(i_0)$. Note $x^\ast(i_0)\in\overline{B_{i_1}}\subseteq B_{i_0}$.

For $n\le m$, membership $i_m\in\mathrm{Small}(m)$ supplies rationals with $b_n-a_n<2^{-m}$ and $\overline{B_{i_m}}\subseteq f_n^{-1}[a_n,b_n]$, so $f_n(x^\ast)\in[a_n,b_n]$. Thus $f_n(x^\ast)$ is computable uniformly in $n$ and in the construction, and therefore so is
\[
\rho\big(x^\ast(i_0),x^\ast(i_0')\big)=\sum_n2^{-n}\big|f_n(x^\ast(i_0))-f_n(x^\ast(i_0'))\big| ,
\]
as the series converges effectively.

Let $(\alpha_r)_{r\in \mathbb{N}}$ enumerate $x^\ast(i_0)$ as $i_0$ ranges over $\Omega$. Any nonempty open $U$ contains a basic $B_{i_0}$ which is nonempty, hence in $\Omega$, and $x^\ast(i_0)\in B_{i_0}\subseteq U$, proving that the sequence is dense

The family $\{B_i : i\in\mathrm{Small}(k)\cap\Omega\}$ is c.e. and covers $X$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:small}. Computable compactness yields a finite subcover indexed by $i^{(1)},\dots,i^{(r)}\in\mathrm{Small}(k)\cap\Omega$. Each $B_{i^{(t)}}$ has $\rho$-diameter at most $2^{-k+2}$ and contains the special point $x^\ast(i^{(t)})$, so the balls $B_\rho(x^\ast(i^{(t)}),2^{-k+2})$ cover $X$. As $k$ is arbitrary this establishes computable compactness of the the computable metric space $(X,\rho,(\alpha_r))$.

The identity $(X,\tau)\to(X,\rho)$ is computable (and thus continuous) by Proposition \ref{prop:metricfn}. Its inverse is computable (and thus continuous) by Corollary~\ref{cor:inverse}, $X$ being computably compact and $(X,\rho)$ computably Hausdorff.
